en: Homage to Vajrasattva!

[I.1] Those belonging to the lineage of the realization of the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayānābhisamayagotra*), who are learned in the scriptures, having ascended to the Vajra Vehicle through association with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), enter into the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the yoga of the imagined deity. Turning away from the six-pointed exegesis (*ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*), they propitiate a Vajra Master and, having heard the *Śrī Guhyasamāja Mahāyogatantra* by way of the literal meaning of the words, extract it from the tantra for the sake of awakening the ignorant. Following the instructions as they have received them, they also compose the auxiliary practices (*sādhanāṅga*) of the yoga of the imagined deity through various specific arrangements of terminology.
[2] In this regard, some Vajrācāryas conceive of the accomplishment of Vajrasattva through the sequence of the moon and vajra (candravajrakrama),
while others do so through the sequence of the arising of existence (bhavotpattikrama).
Some [practitioners] conceive the accomplishment of Vajrasattva through the sequence of the fivefold manifest enlightenment, while others do so through the instantaneous sequence.
Regarding the deities of the maṇḍala, some maintain that there are thirteen;
some, nineteen;
and others maintain that there is an arrangement of twenty-five deities.
Thus, in this tantra, they bring forth the forms of deities such as Vajrasattva by relying on various causes;
accordingly, they also compose commentaries and word-by-word expositions (*pañjikā*) and teach them to those beings who are to be trained.

Therein, those who have full faith in the Vajrayāna, having obtained their respective traditions through the guidance of faith, practice the yoga of the conceptual deity by means of the sequence of hearing, reflection, and meditation.

[1.3] Having understood this essential point, and having heard the Tantra according to the *Samāja-vyākhyā-tantra* through the lineage of the venerable Nāgārjuna by means of the sixfold method of exposition (*ṣaṭkoṭi-vyākhyā*), and having realized the two stages (*krama-dvaya*), I have extracted in sequence, up to the seventeenth chapter, the sūtras concerning the accomplishment of Vajrasattva—both in their systematic and unsystematic forms—for those who are attached to various types of the generation stage (*utpatti-krama*), so that there may be no doubt regarding the practice of the generation stage. Thus, this compendium (*melāpaka*) is composed.

[I.1] First of all, the sequential order for hearing the means of accomplishment is demonstrated: first is the memorization of the mantra; second is the instruction on the ritual placement (*nyāsa*); third is the arrangement of the stations; and fourth is the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*).
Having heard this sequence suitable for the practice and having obtained the command of the Vajra Guru, one should offer an *argha* oblation before one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).

Then, the practitioner, in a favorable location such as a great forest and facing east, sits in the sattva-paryaṅka posture; having generated a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings, he should accomplish the state of Vajrasattva for the sake of the welfare of himself and others, according to the sequence to be described.
The sūtra for this [practice] is: "In regions of great forests adorned with fruits, flowers, and the like, or on a solitary mountain, one should accomplish the compendium of all siddhis."
Thus [it is said].

Immediately thereafter, the practitioner, having removed ordinary ego-grasping through the resolve for emptiness (*śūnyatādhimokṣa*), should instantaneously conceive of himself in the form of Mahāvajradhara, white in color. The scriptural authority for this is found in the third chapter: "One should visualize the Buddha-maṇḍala situated in the center of the space-element, a magnificent array of clouds of light rays, with a radiance equal to the blazing of the Buddhas."
Thus [it is said].

Then, according to the method of the *Jñānapradīpavajrasamādhi* taught in the first chapter, one should utter the mantra *Vajradhrk*. Having visualized oneself as Akṣobhya—black in color, with three faces and six arms—standing before oneself, one should then cause him to enter into one's own body by the analogy of milk and water, and [visualize] oneself as being the color of sapphire.

[Regarding] the *Samāja*, [the text] from the seventeenth chapter onwards is the Sūtra on the production of Vajrasattva in various ways. It concerns the sequence for hearing the means (*upāyikā*) of the sādhana. One should meditate upon the form of the six vajras, which is the color of sapphire (*indranīlavarṇa*), according to the method (*nyāya*) for the benefit of oneself and others, situated before oneself (*ātmapurastha*). One should meditate upon that very [form] instantly (*jhaṭiti*). [The text reads: *mahāvajradhara*; [the Tibetan translation is] *rdo rje ’chan chen po’i*. [The text reads] *tenā*; [the Tibetan translation is] *des na*. [The text reads] *ātmapurastham*; [the Tibetan translation is] *bdag ñid kyi mdun du*. [The text reads] *punas tam*; [this is not in the Tibetan]. [The text reads] *nyāyenā*; [the Tibetan translation is] *tshul gyis*. [The text reads] *indranīlavarnnam*; [the Tibetan translation is] *indra nīla’i mdog can*. One should meditate upon the form of the six vajras.

The sūtra for this is in the first chapter: "The Vidyā-puruṣa of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, through the supreme state of union with the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Akṣobhya, in the form of black, white, and red, caused himself to sit upon the Body-Speech-Mind Vajra of all Tathāgatas within the Body-Speech-Mind Vajra of all Tathāgatas."

Thus, the mantra practitioner established in the *dveṣavajra-samādhi* should utter the syllable *Dīrgha* (DĪḤ) and visualize the ten wrathful deities, such as Yamāntaka and the rest, born from it—each with three faces, six arms, and hands busy with various weapons—stationed in the ten directions, intent on threatening the wicked.
The sūtra for this is found in the thirteenth chapter: "The wrathful ones born in the abode of hatred are eternally intent on slaying;
they are accomplished for the purpose of slaying by the practitioner who possesses the supreme dharma."
Thus [it is said].

Then, having emanated a second Nisumbharāja from the lower position of the first Nisumbharāja, and perceiving him standing before her in the form of a servant seeking an order, she should give the command with the *lokeśvaracaturhaṃkāra* mantra.
There, this is the mantra: *oṃ sumbha ni- sumbha hūṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ ānaya ho bhagavanvidyārāja hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, one should visualize [the practitioner] going to the ten directions to seize Nisumbharāja, the lord of obstacles for the gods and others, by drawing him in with a hook and binding his throat with a noose, and then presenting him to the ten wrathful deities.

Then, having stationed Amṛtakuṇḍalin as a second emanation at the northern gate, one should manifest oneself in the form of the ten *kīla*s and visualize them falling upon the heads of the ten lords of obstacles.
Then, one should meditate on Nisumbharāja rising up and striking [the kīlas] with a vajra-hammer while reciting the mantra.

In this regard, the mantra is as follows: *Oṃ gha gha gha gha ghātaya ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ phaṭ kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ vajrakīla vajradhara ājñāpayati | sarvavighnānāṃ kāya-caturdaśapaṭa-niśumbha° svapura-hṛdaye*.

With the form of a servant (*kinkara*), namely the form of Gnod-mdzes (*Gnāpadeva*), [he says] *kinkara*, *sumbha niśumbha*, *ho hūṃ*. Having drawn the ten directions with the hook (*aṅkuśa*), having bound them... having bound them.

The second [is] Amṛtakundalin. In the second [position], the form of ten stakes (*daśakīla*) and the form of Śaktilaka; the form of the ten stakes for the lords, for the lords, for the supreme lord: *niśumbha niśumbha gha gha gha gha gha 4 gha gha gha gha ghātaya ghātaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ; hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*. O Vajrakīla, he commands: "Command all obstacles, all the wicked ones, and the obstacles of speech and mind—pin them with the vajra! hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ."
One should visualize the great wrathful Vajrāmṛta as a vajra-stake, blazing with a brilliant radiance of sparks; one should then drive it into the ten directions.
Thus [it is said].
Then, with the *Ṭakkirāja* mantra, one should visualize four enclosures—of iron, water, fire, and wind—in sequence on the outside.
This is the mantra: *Ṭakka hūṃ jaḥ*.

Then, with the syllable *Bhūṃ*, one should visualize a vajra-lattice above, situated like a *caitya* atop the iron enclosure. With the three-syllable mantra, one should visualize the armor; and with the syllable *Hūṃ*, one should visualize the ground as consisting of a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*).

In this way, preceded by the ritual procedures for binding the directions with boundaries, the vajra-fence, the vajra-canopy, and so forth, one should meditate. Regarding its benefits, the sūtra states in the thirteenth chapter: "The undertaking born of meditation—whichever place one practices in, by abiding through this yoga of meditation, one is empowered by the Buddhas."
Thus.

Then, with the verse on *bodhicitta* spoken in the second chapter, one should cause the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) and the triple world to enter into suchness (*tathatā*). Here is that verse: "In non-existence, there is no cultivation; cultivation is indeed not cultivation. Kīlaya kīlaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ. [The mantra continues: *rakṣācakram*, *cittavajram*, *cittam*, *tsitta badzra cittavajram*. *Kīlaya kīlaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.

*Trayodaśa* (thirteen), *daśona-daśa* (ten minus ten), *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* twice; *phaṭ*, *hūṃ hūṃ*. One should visualize (*vibhāvayet*) and manifest (*prabhāvayet*) the Wrathful King (*krodharāja*). One should bury (*nikhanet*) [the mantra] and cause it to be buried in the ten directions (*daśadiśāgre*), at the edge of the ten mandalas (*daśadig-maṇḍalāgre*). [The mantra is: *prakāra*, *takki takki*, *daśadiśāgre*, *prakāra*, *ra hūṃ*, *pañjara*, *pañjara*, and the armor (*kavaca*) with the three syllables.
By means of the syllable *hūṃ*, the ground becomes composed of a crossed vajra; by means of the three syllables, one is armored.

With *hūṃ*, the portion of the earth [is visualized] as being of the nature of a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*); with the three syllables, the armor; with *hūṃ*, the portion of the earth as being of the nature of a crossed vajra; with the mantra of the three syllables, the armor. The vajra-fence (*vajraprākāra*), the fence (*prākāra*)—the former, the former—the benefit (*ānuśaṃsā*). Thus: "Existence would not be existence; meditation is not perceived."
Thus, this too is the supreme protection.

In the midst of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), one should visualize a bow-shaped wind-mandala (*vāyumaṇḍala*) from the syllable *yaṃ*; then, having visualized it marked on both sides with two *hūṃ* syllables and two vajras, [one visualizes] above that a triangular fire-mandala (*agnimaṇḍala*) from the syllable *raṃ*, marked with two vajras; and having visualized a water-mandala (*vāruṇamaṇḍala*) marked with two vajras, [one visualizes] again above that a circular [earth-mandala] from the syllable *vaṃ*, and above that a square [earth-mandala] from the syllable *laṃ*. By which meditation is the commitment (*samādāna*) of the *iṣṭadevatā* empowered? It is empowered by the verse spoken in this chapter: "Meditation is indeed non-meditation; existence would be existence through the absence of existence and non-existence; [this is] the ultimate. Having dissolved the four mandalas, one should meditate upon the earth-mandala alone. Regarding this, the sūtra in the eleventh chapter says: "One should contemplate the mandala born of all vajras situated in the center of the space-vajra; there, one should visualize the syllable *śrūṃ*, which brings forth a mass of vajras."
Thus it is said.

Having thus completed the foundational maṇḍala, one should [visualize] a peaked pavilion by means of the syllable *śrūṃ*; it is square, with four doors, adorned with four archways, provided with four boundary lines, and embellished with eight pillars.
Adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, and featuring jeweled half-moons set with diamonds, it is inlaid with diamond-gems at the joints of the doors and the gate-towers.
"With pot-shaped pillars, great vajras, and a pinnacle like a bird's head, adorned with bells and banners, and decorated with chowries and the like"—thus it is said.
Regarding this, the sūtra in the eighth chapter states: "A beautiful, four-cornered caitya, one hundred yojanas in extent, consisting of the four jewels, transparent and naturally stainless."

Having visualized such an excellent palace, distinguished by these qualities and transcending those of gods and humans, situated upon the surface of the earth-mandala; having established the seats of the moon, sun, and so forth; and having personally cast off ordinary ego-conception, one should instantly contemplate oneself as Mahāvajradhara—sapphire-colored, with three faces and six arms, holding a vajra, a wheel, and a lotus in the right hands, and a bell, a wish-fulfilling jewel, and a sword in the left hands—in the posture of *sampuṭa-yoga*, seated in the *sattva-paryaṅka* on a lotus and moon seat within the central maṇḍala.

Then, having visualized Vairocana in the east, Ratnasambhava in the south, Amitābha in the west, Amoghasiddhi in the north, Locanā in the southeast, Māmakī in the southwest, Pāṇḍaravāsinī in the northwest, and Tārā in the northeast within the inner maṇḍala; one should contemplate Rūpavajrā in the southeast of the second enclosure, Śabdavajrā in the southwest, Gandhavajrā in the northwest, Rasavajrā in the northeast, and in the center Sparśavajrā, who stands embracing Vajrasattva.

Likewise, in the third enclosure, one should meditate on Maitreya and Kṣitigarbha on the eastern frieze; Vajrapāṇi and Khagarbha on the southern frieze; Lokeśvara and Mañjughoṣa on the western frieze; and Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin and Samantabhadra on the northern frieze. At the eastern gate, Yamāntaka; at the southern gate, Aparājita; at the western gate, Hayagrīva; and at the northern gate, Amṛtakuṇḍalin. In the southeast, Acala; in the southwest, Ṭakkirāja; in the northwest, Nīladaṇḍa; and in the northeast, Mahābala. Above is Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, and below is Niṣumbharāja.

The sūtra for this is in the first chapter: "It is transparent and its very nature is such, yet it appears in various forms on all sides; it is filled with clouds of Buddhas and agitated by a dense mass of sparks; it is endowed with mandalas such as the transparent one—the city of all the Tathāgatas. Thus [it is said].

[II.1.3] Having thus resolved upon the emanation of the thirty-two deities in the external maṇḍala, one should then assign them within one’s own body-maṇḍala: the five Buddhas as the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*); the knowledge-deities (*vidyādevatā*) as the nature of the elements (*dhātu*); Rūpavajrā and the others as the nature of the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*), such as form; the Bodhisattvas as the nature of the sense-bases (*āyatana*); and the Wrathful Kings (*krodharāja*) as the nature of the limbs.

The sūtra for this is in the seventeenth chapter: "In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed as the five Buddhas; the vajra-sense bases themselves are the supreme maṇḍala of the Bodhisattvas. Earth is called Locanā, the water element is known as Māmakī, fire is called Pāṇḍarā, and wind is proclaimed as Tārā. The mantrin should always meditate upon the deities through form, sound, and the other [sensory objects]. Thus it is said.

Having understood this significance, the Blessed One, in the *Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālasaṃvara-mahāyogatantra*, spoke thus to Maitreya, Vajrapāṇi, Ākāśagarbha, Lokeśvara, Mañjughoṣa, and Mañjuśrī, who were stationed at the southern gate, the western gate, the upper [gate], and the northern gate respectively, as well as to Uṣṇīṣa and Nisumbha: "One should always meditate upon forms, sounds, and so forth as being the deities themselves."

One should arrange the Bodhisattvas according to the nature of the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and Rūpavajrā and the others according to the nature of the objects such as form (*rūpa*). One should contemplate that the Bodhisattvas are of the nature of the sense-bases, and Rūpavajrā and the others are of the nature of the objects such as form. In brief, in the seventeenth chapter, having understood the deities to be the very vajra-sense-bases through the vajra-sense-bases themselves, he said: "For those whose yoga is directed toward what is not the reality, the yoga consisting of a reflected image arises in relation to the deities, such as in cast [images] and so forth. For those whose yoga is directed toward the true reality, what is the use of focusing on a deity? Through the self-yoga of one's own commitment (*samaya*), the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*) is accomplished. Indeed, the self is all Buddhahood and all Sauritva (the state of a Hero). Therefore, with every effort, one should always worship the self. Thus it is said.

Thus, having caused the outer maṇḍala to enter into the body maṇḍala, and having resolved that one's own body maṇḍala is composed of the atoms of all Tathāgatas, one should again cause the deities of the body maṇḍala—who are by nature the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—to dissolve in their proper order into the ultimate maṇḍala. Then, with the mantra from the third chapter, *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, one should solidify the dharmakāya.

The sūtra for this is in the seventh chapter [of the *Tattvajñānasamsiddhi*]: "By means of the ritual, one should drink the semen that flows from the commitment (*samaya*) out of a desire for the fruit. One should slay the array of Tathāgatas and thereby most certainly attain accomplishment."

Thus, having washed away all the stains of the afflictions by means of the object of emptiness, one should generate oneself in the form of Vajrasattva Mahāmudrā through this sequence. This is the sequence: from ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), there arises a sun mandala; above that, a moon mandala; and again above that, a red eight-petaled lotus. Having placed the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* one above the other upon the lotus, and having withdrawn everything into that, one should meditate on mind-only (*cittamātra*) transformed into the shape of a full moon mandala. Having internalized within it the entire world of the moving and the stationary, one should stabilize one’s own jewel-like mind with the mantra taught in the third chapter: *oṃ dharmadhātusvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
Thus, this is the first yoga.
Illuminating this point, he says: "In the context of restraint (*saṃvara*), the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) consisting of mere gnosis (*jñāna-mātra*) is designated as 'yoga'."

"Then, above the lunar disc, the three syllables; from that, the vajra; from the vajra, Mahāvajradhara is born according to the rite, by the name of the rite. Having clearly manifested [him] through the self-yoga and one's own commitment (*svasamaya*), and through the self-yoga and the commitment, [one attains] the state of a Sun-god (*sauritva*) from the self-yoga and one's own commitment, by means of diligent effort, indeed, through the self and diligent effort."

One should worship, one should worship the outer maṇḍala within the body-maṇḍala; in the outer maṇḍala, [it is] enclosed, not enclosed, or constructed. In the maṇḍala, according to the sequence, according to the proper order, with this mantra mentioned in the third chapter—*om*—having washed the feet, the sequence here is as follows:
*om*, having placed the full moon, *jagat*.

The *om* mentioned in the third chapter; the *om* mentioned in the third chapter; the *om* mentioned in the third chapter. This is the first yoga; this is the first yoga. "Ajaya" means *om*. This is the first application (*upayoga*), the first yoga.
One should meditate on one's own form as being white in color, according to the statement in the fifteenth chapter. This is the second *anuyoga*.

Regarding this, the sūtra states in the eleventh chapter: "The visualization of the Mahāmudrā should be performed by means of the supreme mantras of the three vajra-syllables, using the Wisdom-Vajra, which brings about the realization of all enlightenment."

Having thus accomplished oneself as the *saṃbhogakāya* through the sequence of yoga and its application (*yogānuyoga*), one should, for the sake of sentient beings like those in their final existence, produce oneself as the *nirmāṇakāya* by entering into the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandhadhātvāyatana*) according to this sequence. In this regard, the sequence is as follows: having placed a white syllable *oṃ*, whose nature is Vairocana, upon the head, one should cause it to enter the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Likewise, having placed a red syllable *āḥ*, whose nature is Amitābha, in the mouth, one should cause it to enter the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).

Having placed the syllable *hūṃ*, black in color and of the nature of Akṣobhya, in the heart, one should cause the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) to enter it. One should contemplate oneself as the Vajra[-being] within the Vajra[-realm]. [Regarding] the eleventh chapter, the tenth chapter, the final-existence [Bodhisattva], the Bodhisattva of the final existence, all beings, for the sake of sentient beings like those in their final existence—[one should contemplate] the red-colored [syllable] as red, the black-colored as black, and the black as Akṣobhya. Having placed the syllable *svā*, yellow in color and of the nature of Ratnasambhava, at the navel, one should cause the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) to enter it.
Having placed the green-colored syllable HĀḤ, whose nature is Amoghasiddhi, upon the two feet, one should cause the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) to enter.

Having assigned Locanā as "delight in delusion" by way of the nature of the earth element, Māmakī as "delight in hatred" by way of the nature of the water element, Pāṇḍarā as "delight in passion" by way of the nature of the fire element, and Tārā as "delight in the vajra" by way of the nature of the wind element, one should conceive of hardness, fluidity, heat, and motility.

One should assign Kṣitigarbha to the *thalī* (the pit of the stomach) by way of the nature of the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*); Oṃ Vajrapāṇi, by way of the nature of the ear-base (*śrotrāyatana*); Oṃ Ākāśagarbha, by way of the form of the nose-base (*ghrāṇāyatana*); Oṃ Lokeśvara, by way of the nature of the tongue-base (*jihvāyatana*); Hūṃ Mañjuśrī, by way of the nature of the mind-base (*manaāyatana*); and Oṃ Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, by way of the nature of the body-base (*kāyāyatana*). Having thus assigned them, one should visualize the divine eyes and so forth.
One should assign the seed-syllable Maiṃ as Maitreya by way of the nature of the sinews (*snāyu*).
One should place Samantabhadra together with his seed-syllable by means of the essential nature of the joints of the entire body.

Thus, having filled the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*) through the empowerment of the mantra, one should recite ten long *hūṃ* syllables. *Moharatī*, *moharatī*; *dveṣaratī*, *dveṣaratī*; *vajraratī*, *vajraratī*; *rāgaratī*, *rāgaratī*. *Tārām*, *tārām*, let [them] become fluid, heat, *thlim*, *thlim*, *thlīm*. *Kṣitigarbham*, *kṣitigarbham*, the seed-syllable of Kṣitigarbha, by way of its own form, by way of its intrinsic nature. *Lokeśvaram*, *lokeśam*, Lokeśvara, by way of the form of the tongue-base, by way of the nature of the tongue-base, by way of the form of the tongue-base. *Snāyu*, *snāyu*, by way of its own form, by way of its form, by way of its intrinsic nature. *Divyalocanādim*, *divyacakṣurādim*, Locanā and the others, by way of their intrinsic nature, by way of their nature, one should place them, one should arrange them, through the empowerment of the empowerment. *Hūṃkāra*, *hūṃkāra*, *hūṃkāra*.

One should assign the wrathful deities to the limbs, beginning with the arms, according to this sequence: Yamāntaka on the right arm, Aparājita on the left arm, Hayagrīva in the mouth, Amṛtakuṇḍalin in the secret place, Acala on the right forearm, Ṭakkirāja on the left forearm, Nīladaṇḍa on the right knee, Mahābala on the left knee, Uṣṇīṣacakravartin on the crown of the head, and Niṣumbharāja on the two feet; having thus assigned them, one should cause them to enter the ten directions.

The sūtra for this [is found] in the first chapter: "He empowered the form of the Great Knowledge-Person (*mahāvidyāpuruṣa*), which is the empowerment of the mantras of all Tathāgatas. As soon as it was thus empowered, that very Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajra-Bodhicitta, appeared to all the Tathāgatas in the form of three faces.
This is the third *atiyoga*.

Thus, the practitioner, having removed his own innate ego through the three yogas and having manifested the form of Śrī Vajrasattva, should perform the fourth, the Mahāyoga, for the purpose of removing the conceptualizations of both the deity being formed and the fully accomplished deity. In that regard, having meditated on a white syllable OṂ at the crown of the head, one should contemplate the array of Locanās produced from it within the hollow of space by means of the application of lordship.

Then, instantaneously, by means of the application of mastery over the Vairocana-array, having seen [it] in the intermediate space, [he visualizes] the twelve-petaled lotus; the syllable *amṛta* (or *amṛtakundali*) on the wind [element];

*oṃ* on the left arm; *pā* on the two feet; *ya* on the right [arm]; *nisumbha* on the [left] leg; and the *tathāgata-mantra-adhiṣṭhāna* on the body. Thus, the Blessed One, as the third [deity], through the threefold yoga of himself, [perceives] again the array of the deities being produced from the vase, [established] in his mastery.
Having reflected thus, one should make the request with two *loktagāthās*.
Therein, this is the verse: "The glorious bearer of the Buddha-body, cultivated through the indivisibility of the three vajras—may he today grant me the state of empowerment as the Body-Vajra."
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who have realized the indivisibility of the three vajras,

The Blessed One Śākyamuni, having performed all these deeds, descended from the supreme realm of Tuṣita; he manifested the form of one free from passion, established those of the *śrāvaka* lineage upon the path of the *śrāvakas*, and further elucidated the path of the perfections (*pāramitāmārga*) for the Mahāyāna bodhisattvas. Alternatively, having emanated a Knowledge-Seal (*jñānamudrā*) from one’s own heart and performed union with her, one should act for the benefit of sentient beings through the single emanation of the mantra. in the center, one should visualize Sparśavajrā abiding in perfect embrace with Vajrasattva. Likewise, on the eastern ledge of the third tier are Maitreya and Kṣitigarbha.
On the southern ledge are Vajrapāṇi and Ākāśagarbha; on the western ledge are Lokeśvara and Mañjughoṣa;
and on the northern ledge are Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin and Samantabhadra.
At the eastern gate is Yamāntaka; at the southern gate is Aparājita;
at the western gate is Hayagrīva.
At the northern gate is Amṛtakuṇḍalin; in the southeast is Acala;
and in the southwest is Takkirāja.
In the northwest is Nīladaṇḍa;
in the northeast is Mahābala;
and above is Uṣṇīṣacakravartin.
Below, one should visualize the King Sumbharāja.
Regarding this, the sūtra states in the first chapter:
"The very essence of that clarity."
Possessing various forms on all sides,
perfectly endowed with clouds of Buddhas,
blazing and swirling with rays of light.
It possesses the mandalas of clarity and so forth;
it should be known as the abode of all the Tathāgatas.
Having thus cultivated the conviction that the thirty-two deities have been emanated within the external maṇḍala,
one should further [visualize] these as being within the maṇḍala of one’s own body: the five Buddhas by nature of the aggregates, and the vidyā goddesses by nature of the elements.
The Bodhisattvas are to be arrayed by means of the nature of the sense bases (*āyatana*), and the Kings of Wrath (*krodharāja*) are to be arrayed by means of the nature of the limbs.
As for the five aggregates (*skandha*), in brief:
They are renowned as the five Buddhas;
the vajra sense bases themselves are the supreme maṇḍala of the bodhisattvas.
Earth is renowned as Locanā; the water element is known as Māmakī;
fire is called Pāṇḍaravāsinī.
The wind is renowned as Tārā;
one should always meditate on form, sound, and so forth as being the deity itself.
Thus it was said.
Having realized this essential point, from the *Mahāyoga Tantra: The Union with All Buddhas, the Vajraḍāka Net* (*Sarvabuddhasamāyogadākinījālasaṃvara*):
The Blessed One said:
"The yogin who does not conceptualize that very reality,
yet perceives it as the deity itself— "
Does the yoga of the nature of the reflected image arise from cast metal statues and the like? Or does it arise for the yogi who correctly contemplates that very reality?
What is the use of visualizing [others] as deities?
Through the samaya of self-union,
the supreme unchanging state will be accomplished.
I myself am all the Buddhas, And I am the supreme among them all. Therefore, with every effort,
"One should always worship oneself," it is said.
Thus, having integrated the external maṇḍala into the body maṇḍala,

Having visualized oneself as the body maṇḍala, composed of the subtle atoms of all the Tathāgatas, one should then cause the deities of the body maṇḍala—the natures of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—to dissolve sequentially, thereby entering the ultimate maṇḍala.
One should stabilize this as the dharmakāya with the mantra taught in the third chapter: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ*.
The sūtra for this is from the seventh chapter: "Those who desire the fruit should drink the seminal fluid born of the samaya in accordance with the Dharma."
If one slays the assembly of Tathāgatas,
the most supreme siddhi will be accomplished. Thus, by focusing on emptiness, all stains of the afflictions are cleared away.
Then, one should generate oneself in the form of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Vajrasattva.
By this sequence, from the ultimate truth arises a sun mandala,
and upon that, a moon mandala.
Upon that, on top of an eight-petaled red lotus, one should arrange the three syllables OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ one above the other; from the total condensation of all these, a complete moon maṇḍala arises.
Contemplating this as mind-only, the two—the stable and the moving worlds—are gathered within it.
Then, reciting "OṂ DHARMADHĀTU SVABHĀVA ĀTMAKO ’HAṂ" as taught in the third chapter, this is the first yoga.
This point is clearly taught in the *Cakrasaṃvara*:
"The meditative absorption into mere primordial wisdom is explicitly designated as 'yoga'."
Thus it is said.
Then, upon a moon mandala, there are the three syllables;
from those, a vajra arises.
From the vajra, one should visualize oneself as the Great Vajradhara, white in color.
He is the great king Vajrasattva,
with a radiance equal to that of Vairocana.
This is because it is stated in the fifteenth chapter;
second is the subsequent yoga (*anuyoga*).
Its sūtra is from the eleventh chapter:
Through the supreme mantra of the three vajra syllables,
the meditation on Mahāmudrā is called the Wisdom Vajra.
It is said: "That which equally generates all awakenings.
Thus, through the stages of yoga and subsequent yoga, one generates oneself as the saṃbhogakāya.
For the sake of sentient beings in their final existence, one should generate oneself as the nirmāṇakāya through this sequence of entering into the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
This is the sequence: having placed a white OṂ, the nature of Vairocana, upon the crown of the head, one should cause it to enter the aggregate of form.
One should place a red ĀḤ, the nature of Amitābha, at the throat and cause it to enter the aggregate of perception.
One should place a black HŪṂ, the nature of Akṣobhya, at the heart and cause it to enter the aggregate of consciousness.
One should place a yellow SVĀ, the nature of Ratnasambhava, at the navel and cause it to enter the aggregate of feeling.
Having placed the green syllable HĀ, the nature of Amoghasiddhi, upon the two feet, one should cause it to enter the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
By means of the words MOHARATI, Locanā enters by way of the nature of the earth element;
by means of the words DVEṢARATI, Māmakī enters by way of the nature of the water element.
By means of *rāgarati*, one [visualizes] Pāṇḍaravāsinī, who is of the nature of the fire element;
by means of *vajrarati*, one [visualizes] Tārā, who is of the nature of the wind element.
Having thus arranged them, one should clearly contemplate [them] as solidity, fluidity, heat, and motility.

[1.3.3] Having established the seed-syllable OṂ of Kṣitigarbha as the nature of the eye sense-field, the seed-syllable OṂ of Vajrapāṇi as the nature of the ear sense-field, the seed-syllable OṂ of Ākāśagarbha as the nature of the nose sense-field, the seed-syllable AṂ of Lokeśvara as the nature of the tongue sense-field, the seed-syllable HŪṂ of Mañjuśrī as the nature of the mental sense-field, and the seed-syllable OṂ of Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin as the nature of the body sense-field, one should thoroughly visualize them as the divine eyes and so forth.
One should place the seed-syllable of Maitreya, *mo*, upon the nature of the sinews.
One should place the seed-syllable of Samantabhadra, *saṃ*, upon all the joints of the body.

[01.3.4] Thus, having been blessed by the mantra, one fills the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-fields (*āyatana*). Then, from a long *HŪṂ*, the ten wrathful deities (*krodha*) are to be arranged upon the limbs, such as the hands, according to this sequence: Yamāntaka on the right hand; Aparājita on the left hand; Hayagrīva in the mouth; Amṛtakuṇḍalī in the secret place; Acala on the right rib; Ṭakkirāja on the left rib; Nīladaṇḍa on the right knee; Mahābala on the left knee; Uṣṇīṣacakravartin on the crown of the head; and Sumbharāja on the two feet. Having thus arranged them, they should be projected into the ten directions.

The sūtra for this is found in the first chapter: "When the body of the Great Vidyā-puruṣa was blessed by the mantras of all the Tathāgatas, immediately upon that blessing, that very Bodhicitta-vajra appeared in the form of the three faces of the Tathāgatas. Thus it is said.
The mantra for this is as follows:
*oṃ sarvatathāgatavāgvajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ*.
Then, again, one should visualize a black syllable *hūṃ* at the hub of the vajra at one’s own heart.
Visualizing a host of Māmakīs born from that in the sky,
one should look upon a host of Akṣobhyas in the intermediate space as before, and offer this supplication in verse:
"O Glorious Holder of the Vajra Mind,"
Through meditating on the three indivisible vajras,
may the Vajra Mind grant its blessing so that I may become habituated to it this very day.
Through meditating on the three indivisible vajras, may the Buddhas residing in the ten directions grant their blessing today so that I may become habituated [to it].
"Please act with the Vajra Mind!

As soon as this supplication is made, one should visualize that—as previously explained—one melts through the fire of non-dual great passion and enters the heart center in the form of black light rays, thereby attaining mastery over the mind. Then, one should stabilize this state with the following verse: "What is the mind of Samantabhadra..."
May I too become like the wise Lord of Secrets, and may I be just like him who upholds the enlightened mind.
Thus it is said.
Then, one should cultivate the pride of non-dual form with this mantra:
*oṃ sarvatathāgatacittavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
By inserting those three families in that manner, one blesses the body, speech, and mind individually;
then, one should perform this blessing into the state of Great Vajradhara through the nature of the indivisibility of the three vajras with the mantra:
*oṃ sarvatathāgata kāyavāk citta vajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ*.
The sūtra for this is from the second chapter:
"Bhagavān, the mind has the aspect of the body, and the body has the aspect of the mind."
It is taught that one should generate [the deity] in a manner similar to the mental and verbal expressions of speech.
Because it is generated by way of the vajra-samādhi arising from the commitments (samaya) as taught in the first chapter, it is called the "commitment-being" (samayasattva).
Having thus generated the commitment-being with three faces and six arms,

At his heart, one should visualize a two-armed wisdom being (*jñānasattva*) of red color, whose entire body is satiated through the union of the *kha-sbyor* (the embrace), and then visualize the Lord upon one’s own crown. The sūtra for this is from the twelfth chapter:

By means of the union of the self, one consecrates the self. By means of that consecration, [one becomes] the supreme, the *ātmaka*, the *ātmaka* of the union of the mouth. Possessing the excellence of all aspects, the vajra body, speech, and mind of the self, the wisdom of the samaya resides in the heart.
Upon the crown of the Holder of the Supreme Vajra,
this is the sublime samaya that satisfies all the Buddhas.
"It is the activity of all samayas,
which accomplishes all siddhis," so it was said.

Thus, having visualized the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) at the heart of the commitment-being (*samayasattva*), one should visualize at the heart of the wisdom-being the syllable *HŪṂ*, known as the concentration-being (*samādhisattva*). This is to be contemplated as that which constantly arises like a great lamp, appearing like a mass of light for the purpose of destroying the darkness of ignorance.
The sūtra for this is found in the eleventh chapter:
Abiding in the center of the Buddha-maṇḍala,
having meditated on the syllable HŪṂ at the heart,
one should settle the mind in the bindu.
This is the Mahāyoga.
Thus, through the four yogas, one generates the supreme King of Samādhis, which is the nature of the perfection of one's own welfare, characterized by the identity of the three beings.
Now, for the sake of the perfect benefit of others, we shall enter the section teaching the samādhi known as the Supreme Sovereign Maṇḍala.
The Blessed One Śākyamuni, having performed all [deeds], descended from the supreme abode of Tuṣita; having attained omniscience, he manifested the appearance of one free from passion.
Those of the śrāvaka lineage were established on the level of the śrāvakas.

Furthermore, having clarified all the modes of the *pāramitās* for those sentient beings of the Mahāyāna, [the Buddha] entered the meditative absorption known as "The Mode of Great Passion," which was taught in the first chapter for the purpose of demonstrating this awakening born of passion to those who have superior devotion to the profound. Likewise, a practicing yogi, having first performed the preliminary application, likewise enters that state in order to thoroughly demonstrate liberation through desire to those sentient beings who engage in passion.
One should abide by means of this samādhi that enjoys all desires, according to the sequence taught in the seventeenth chapter.
In that regard, the sequence is as follows:
having found an external mudrā endowed with all the requisite marks and well-trained in mantra and tantra, one should place her before oneself and examine her five families.
Then, preceded by the union of the vajra and lotus, one joins the two organs together.
From the bodhicitta, one emanates the maṇḍala wheel of Akṣobhya and the other deities;
through their respective meditative absorptions, one purifies the afflictions such as hatred of sentient beings, and then withdraws them once again.

One should cause [the deity] to enter the maṇḍala of one’s own body. Alternatively, having clearly emanated the wisdom mudrā at the heart and entered into union with her, one should accomplish the welfare of sentient beings by emanating a mantra.
The great goddess residing in the heart,
who brings about the descent of yoga for yogis,
and who gives rise to the union of the Buddhas.
This is because it is stated in the *Sarvarahasyatantra*: "She is renowned as Vajradhātvīśvarī.
The sūtra for this is spoken in the seventh chapter:
Having found a most enchanting queen who has reached the age of sixteen,
[one should empower her] by means of the three stages.
One should begin the offering in a secluded place;
one should clearly visualize Locanā, the supreme consort of the Tathāgata.
"By the union of the two organs, the siddhi of Buddhahood is attained.
Having thus established certainty regarding the mudrās of both outer and inner nature, the sequence for examining the five families shall be taught.
Oṃ is at the crown of the head;
Āḥ is at the mouth;
Hūṃ is at the heart.
Svā is at the navel;
Hā is placed on the two feet.
Locanā and the others, whose nature consists of the four elements, are to be placed [therein].
One should arrange Rūpavajrā and the others according to the nature of the sense bases, such as the eyes.
Furthermore, one should arrange the Queens of the Wrathful Goddesses on her limbs, such as the hands;
specifically, Vetālī is on her right hand.
On the left hand is Aparājitā;
in the mouth is Bhṛkuṭī; at the secret place is Ekajaṭā.
Furthermore, on the right side is Viśvavajrā;
on the left side is Viśvaratnā;
and on the right knee is Viśvapadma.
On the left knee is Viśvakarmā.
By means of the *ātma-ko* [mantra], desire is thoroughly purified.
Through the *samādhi* of Amoghasiddhi, one purifies envy.
Through the *samādhi* of the Bhagavatī Locanā, one pacifies the illnesses and other afflictions of sentient beings. Through the *samādhi* of Māmakī, one performs the rite of enrichment (*puṣṭi*).
One is protected by the *samādhi* of Pāṇḍaravāsī;
one brings others under control by the *samādhi* of Tārā.
The Blessed One himself, having become Vajrarūpā and so forth, generates happiness and mental well-being for sentient beings.

In the same way, that very Blessed One purifies the sense bases (*āyatana*) of sentient beings through the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of bodhisattvas such as Kṣitigarbha; and that very Blessed One threatens the hosts of obstructors in the ten directions through the meditative absorptions of wrathful deities (*krodha*) such as Yamāntaka. Thus it is said: "The Blessed Vajrayogins, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva."
For it is said: "All his enjoyments are the three realms without exception."
This is the second meditative absorption, called the Supreme King of Mandalas.

[V.H] Having thus manifested the thirty-two wheels, through the subtle mode of yoga—[the text here contains various manuscript variants regarding the specific yogic methods]—you are the one who brings great benefit through the supreme commitment (*samaya*) of vajra-desire.
O Protector, supreme heir of the Perfectly Enlightened One, impartial and compassionate one:
if you wish for me to remain alive this day,
please take delight in me, who have become a treasury of many precious qualities.

Having thus praised him with his authentic qualities, he arose through the power of his former aspirations and was extolled by the Tathāgatas with these kings of praises, beginning with "Akṣobhya. This is that praise: "Akṣobhya is the great vajra;
the Vajradhātu is the great sage.
The three supreme vajras are the three maṇḍalas."
Homage and praise to Guhyasvara!
Vairocana, the great purity; Vajra-śānta, the great bliss!
I prostrate to and praise the Teacher, Vajra, who is by nature supremely luminous;
the King of Jewels, most profound.
I prostrate and praise the Stainless Vajra Sky, whose nature is pure and unstained, the Secret Melody.
Great King Vajra Amitābha,
non-conceptual space-holding Vajradhara,
you who have attained the perfection of passion.
I prostrate to and praise the Vajra Speech. Amoghasiddhi, the perfect Buddha,
who fulfills all intentions.
Arisen from the essence of purity,
I prostrate and praise Vajrasattva.
Abiding in the center of the expanse of space,
One should meditate on the arranged maṇḍala;
within its center, one should clearly visualize one's own form as the syllable HŪṂ.
Thus it was said.
Translated from the presence of Gatarakṣita by the translator Lokya Zhönnu Bar.
